I'll start with the negatives: to be honest, in the middle, the game gets slightly (and I do mean slightly) redundant. You do the same things to hack into a server or computer, you find what you're looking for, get out, and complete your contract. But that's really only for the contracts during the middle of the game. When you get into more complicated missions, finding hidden servers and connected devices, everything becomes much more interesting. The repetition never made me feel bored or want to stop playing. 

Also, the game was a bit short. I felt like it could've used more missions and more story, but I'm not sure there was room for that without making the game ACTUALLY feel repetitive, so no problem there. Also, it'll take up as much of your time as you would expect of a $10 (for $7 if you got it on sale like I did) game. 

But these two problems are not at all enough to keep me from recommending this game to others. The story is really engaging, the puzzles are interesting and rewarding (not too straightforward while also not being impossible), and the music and style of the game is on point. If you come from a programming background (specifically using the linux command line), you'll probably be disappointed that this perfectly realistic, but it's obviously not meant to be. It makes you feel like a hacker, it's not an educational tool.

My point is that is game is amazing. This was both my first hacking and text based game, and I still loved it. Please do yourself a favor and play it. 10/10.

Note: I never had any game breaking bugs like many of the negative reviews reported. There were some things that worried me, like aborting a story mission and not knowing if I could pick it up again, but after a quick google search it appeared finishing the mission I aborted for made the mission "spawn" again, so everything was fine.

Pros:
+ A tense (at times) simulation of hacking
+ Interesting missions
+ Abundant hints that helps move things along without excessive hand-holding

Cons:
- A bit short
- Some technical issues, most notably unresponsive keyboard entry (at least on the Mac OS X)
- Missions are scripted, making replayability questionable

Hacknet is a scripted version of Uplink... I think that's the best way to describe it. Where Uplink offers a plot, you can completely ignore it and treat the game as an open-ended simulation. Missions in Uplink are pretty much generated on the fly, which gives you an endless supply of it at the cost of things being repetitive after awhile. Hacknet's missions are more tightly scripted, making it much more interesting but I do question its replayability. 

Both Hacknet and Uplink offers stylized view of hacking. Hacknet is slightly more realistic with the fully functional console (which those of us used to working with Unix-like commands will find completely familiar). If I have one complaint against Hacknet's art is that it seems to be schizophrenic: it can't decide whether to go for a completely realistic look or a completely stylized one; the mix-and-match style somehow feels a bit of a mismatch. Another complaint is that I sometimes find that the keyboard input is unresponsive: characters are sometimes ignored, the Enter key not properly recognized, etc. This can be very frustrating when you are trying to hammer in commands as quickly as possible before you are traced... this does make for some tense moments, though, and makes me wonder whether this is a bug or a feature.

In all, Hacknet provides you a pleasant distraction for a couple of hours, and it may look cool to bystanders when you seem to be frantically typing commands into your computer to hack into some mainframe. It's got its tense moment, provide a moderately challenging puzzles and some laughs (be sure to read some of the text files scattered in the servers you are hacking into).

Recommended.

Wow! I sat down 4 hours ago and started this game and before I knew it I had blazed through the whole thing.

I'm a big fan of hacking games, especially ones that mix pseudo-realistic stuff with fun Hollywood-style flair. Uplink, released in 2001, is still one of my favorite games because no game before or since really hit that sweet spot. Until Hacknet!

This is a compelling, challenging game with a solid framework of simple mechanics that require you to be ever-more precise and fast in your execution. It also features a number of puzzles that never seem unfair, and yet also never insult your intelligence with hand-holding. 

In comparison to Uplink, Hacknet has no RPG elements, for better or worse. I liked doing random missions over and over again in Uplink to grind up cash to buy a faster processor, new software, etc, but I'm sure many people will prefer Hacknet's more direct and explicit design. Actually, the contracts you're sent on don't feel random at all - each one is a unique challenge in some way, and overall the game is far, far less tedious than Uplink.

The story follows a fairly predictable arc, but that's okay. What keeps you playing isn't wondering what will happen next, but what new type of security you'll have to learn to deal with. The flow of new content is paced perfectly. You're not rushed into a bunch of stuff you don't understand, and you're never just killing time.

There are some nitpicks - I think a few of the challenges might overwhelm people that can't or won't use the terminal, and frankly those Bash.org quotes that are everywhere are older than most of the people on Steam.... but this is a fantastic game at a fair price. If you like puzzles, action, and aren't afraid to type out "cat irc_chat.txt", then do yourself a favor and pick this up today.

Okay, so now for the real review:

HACKNET is a game about hacking in a simplified way. You launch your virtual mashine and recieve the message of a dead-man's trigger program from a Hacker who may have died (that's why it's called Dead-man's trigger). The program will give you a fast tutorial about the gameplay, which appears to be like linux terminal based hacking and launching programs you have stolen to crack security measures so you can take control of other virtual maschines, read their data, steal their data and then cover up your trails. So to say, you become a hacker detective; to clean up a big mess.

The background music is good in my opinion, with some catchy songs and an epic boss-battle BGM.

Another plus point is that it is Linux compatible. Linux is a life saver for many old or light maschines so you can easily put that on a netbook and play it on the go... as Windows eats up more resources than most Linux distributions.

[i]HACKNET will feature a multiplayer at the end of this year [2016] in which you're going to hack against your peers. And careful, they may troll you and open your CD tray in real life... if you have one.[/i]

[h1] This game will [b]NOT[/b] show you how hacking actually works. [/h1]

So, this game is simple and easy... avoid using an actual guide for this because the experience of the game as it is is autosufficient, you learn by playing it and you don't need more intel about it other than what the tutorial shows you and what "/help" shows you. It won't challenge you in such a way that you're going to be able to hack anyone after playing this game.

Overall, I'd say it's a great experience, especially for those looking to relive those tense moments from Introversion's old game.

What an excellent game! It feels just raw enought to trick your mind into momentarily believing you are actually hacking something. 

Its very fun to just mess with server info as well; there are lots of easter eggs and ways to mess with the systems. The story is amazing, and feels legitimate all the way. I absolutely reccomend this game to anybody who is remotely into hacking or even role-playing.

tl;dr: It's quite nice. Has very little to do with hacking, but still a fun game to play if you're apt with a shell.

Summary:
Hacknet is a game in which you do various tasks for various people for various reasons. You delete files, fetch passwords, etc. See it as a puzzle game, of sorts.

If you're a bit familiar with InfoSec, you'll find several references to real-life tools like nmap, or real life fuck-up's (like Apple making "alpine" the default password on every iOS device).

Cons:
However, you'll likely be disappointed that the in-game shell isn't nearly as powerful as any comparable real shell and that a lot of realism has been cut away for the sake of gameplay.
Further, a lot of details simply don't add up. Why does the whole world run UNIX with an open SSH port? Why do they have .dll and .exe files on UNIX? And why does it bluescreen? Why do "binary" files contain 1's and 0's when cat'd, instead of the actual ASCII representation? If you're really out for realism, I suggest you to start a real shell and get cracking - but hey, it's just a game, so enjoy.
